CONTROL SYSTEMS · POSTED OCT 8, 2026 · 5 MIN READ

PID control,
one term at a time.

PID control is a practical way to adjust a system from the difference between a desired value and a measured value. Understanding what each term contributes makes tuning more deliberate.

Close the loop around error

Let the reference be the value you want and the measurement be the value the system currently reports. Their difference is the error. A PID controller combines a response to the present error, its accumulated history, and its rate of change:

u(t) = K p e(t) + K i ∫e(t)dt + K d de(t)/dt

Here, the output u is the control action sent to the plant, such as a motor command or heater power. Real implementations often use discrete-time calculations and filter the derivative term.

What the three terms do

  • Proportional (P) responds to the current error. More gain can make correction stronger, but too much can create overshoot or oscillation.
  • Integral (I) accumulates error over time and can remove a persistent offset. It can also keep accumulating while an actuator is saturated, a problem called integral windup.
  • Derivative (D) responds to how quickly the error changes. It can add damping, but measurement noise can make the derivative noisy; filtering is common.

Tune with a measured process

Start with a safe operating range and a clear performance target. A common learning sequence is to establish stable proportional behavior first, add integral action only if steady-state error remains, and consider derivative action if the response needs more damping. Change one gain at a time and record the step response, overshoot, settling time, and steady-state error.

There is no universal set of gains. The right values depend on the plant, sensor, actuator limits, sample time, and operating conditions. Test changes in simulation or a controlled setup before using them on equipment where unexpected motion or heat could cause damage.

Don’t forget the implementation

Check sample timing, output saturation, sensor scaling, sign conventions, and reset behavior. If an actuator cannot deliver the requested output, add an anti-windup strategy so the integral term does not continue growing without useful effect. For digital controllers, derivative filtering and discrete-time formulas affect the result.

PID is a useful starting point, not a substitute for understanding the system. A good tuning record explains the test conditions and trade-offs so the controller can be revisited later.
